modules.title: Money basics: how a rental makes you rich
modules.summary: A rental pays you four ways: cash flow each month, tenants paying down your loan, appreciation over time, and tax breaks. Learn the core words first so every later lesson clicks. Think of the property as a small business with rent coming in and bills going out.
keyPoints: Four profit engines: cash flow, loan paydown, appreciation, tax savings.
Equity = value minus loan. It grows from paydown and appreciation.
Gross rent is the top line; expenses and vacancy come out next.
Leverage magnifies gains and losses alike.

modules.title: Analyze a deal in 10 minutes
modules.summary: Run every property through the same funnel: quick screens first, then real math. Estimate rent, subtract vacancy and operating expenses to get NOI, then subtract the mortgage for cash flow. Cap rate compares properties; cash-on-cash shows your return; DSCR shows if a lender will like it.
keyPoints: Screen fast: 1% rule and 50% rule weed out bad deals.
NOI = rent - vacancy - operating expenses (no mortgage).
Cap rate = NOI / price. Cash-on-cash = yearly cash flow / cash invested.
DSCR = NOI / yearly loan payments; aim for 1.2+.
Budget for CapEx even when nothing is broken.

modules.title: Financing and scaling: loans, refis, BRRRR
modules.summary: Your loan shapes the deal more than almost anything. FHA allows 3.5% down if you live there; conventional needs PMI under 20% down. Avoid loan features that hide risk, like interest-only periods and balloons. Later, refinancing and BRRRR turn built-up equity into the down payment for the next property.
keyPoints: FHA: 3.5% down, must live there, 1-4 units.
Conventional under 20% down adds PMI until equity builds.
Interest-only and balloon loans lower payments now, raise risk later.
Cash-out refi turns equity into cash for the next deal.
BRRRR: buy below value, rehab, rent, refi, repeat. LLCs come later.

modules.title: Your first property: the house hack
modules.summary: House hacking means you live in the home and rent the other rooms or units. Owner-occupied loans keep the down payment small, and roommates cover most of the mortgage. Get pre-approved, know your DTI, run the numbers with your own room left empty, and plan closing costs and reserves before you offer.
keyPoints: Rent the other rooms; your housing cost drops toward zero.
Lenders check DTI; pay down debts before applying.
Run numbers as if you move out later: is it still a good rental?
Budget closing costs (a few % of price) on top of the down payment.
Get inspection and title checked before closing.

modules.title: Tenants, operations and risk
modules.summary: Good operations protect cash flow. Screen every applicant with the same written criteria and follow fair housing law. Use a written lease, collect a deposit, and track everyone on a rent roll. Fix small problems fast. Keep reserves and proper insurance, and do not borrow so much that one vacancy breaks you.
keyPoints: Same written screening rules for everyone: income, history, references.
Fair Housing Act bans discrimination on 7 protected classes.
Lease + deposit + rent roll = clean records.
Reserves cover vacancy and repairs; aim for months, not weeks.
Over-leverage is the classic way investors lose properties.

modules.title: Taxes and records
modules.summary: Rental income and expenses go on Schedule E. The building, not the land, is depreciated over 27.5 years, which can shelter cash flow on paper. When you rent rooms in your own home, split shared costs between personal and rental use. Keep receipts and mileage. A 1031 exchange can defer gains on investment property.
keyPoints: Report rental income and expenses on Schedule E.
Depreciate the building over 27.5 years; land never depreciates.
Renting rooms in your home: split costs by the rented share.
Save every receipt, lease and mileage log.
1031 exchange: 45 days to identify, 180 to close.

vocab.definition: All rent the property could collect in a period before any expenses or vacancy.
Share of time or rent lost because a unit or room sits empty.
Costs to run the property: taxes, insurance, repairs, utilities, management. Mortgage payments are not included.
Income left after vacancy and operating expenses, before any loan payments.
Money left each month after every expense and the mortgage payment.
NOI divided by price. Compares properties as if bought with all cash.
Yearly cash flow divided by the cash you actually put in.
NOI divided by yearly loan payments. Most lenders want at least 1.2 to 1.25.
Quick screen: monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price. A filter, not a verdict.
Rough guess that operating expenses eat about half of gross rent over time, excluding the mortgage.
vocab.example: $2,400 rent -> plan on about $1,200 in expenses.

vocab.definition: Big, infrequent replacements like a roof, HVAC or water heater. Save for them monthly.
Cash kept aside for vacancies, repairs and surprises so one bad month does not sink you.
The part of the property you own: value minus what you owe.
Increase in a property's value over time. Nice when it happens, risky to count on.
Loan balance divided by property value. Lower LTV means more equity and less risk for the lender.
Monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income. Lenders use it to cap how much you can borrow.
Cash you pay upfront toward the price. The loan covers the rest.
Mortgage not backed by a government agency. Usually needs stronger credit; PMI applies under 20% down.
Government-insured mortgage with as little as 3.5% down. You must live in the home; 1-4 units allowed.
Insurance protecting the lender on conventional loans with under 20% down. You pay it until enough equity builds.
Paying a loan down on a schedule. Early payments are mostly interest; later ones mostly principal.
vocab.example: $200k at 6.5%: payment $1,264, first month $1,083 is interest.

vocab.definition: Principal, interest, taxes and insurance: the full monthly housing payment lenders look at.
Account your lender uses to collect and pay your property taxes and insurance for you.
Loan where early payments cover only interest, so the balance does not shrink.
A large lump sum due at the end of a loan whose regular payments did not pay it off.
vocab.example: 5-year loan ends with $180,000 due at once.

vocab.definition: Replacing your loan with a new one, usually for a lower rate or different term.
New, larger loan that pays off the old one and hands you the difference in cash.
vocab.example: 75% of $300k = $225k loan - $150k owed = $75k cash before costs.

vocab.definition: A licensed professional's estimate of a property's value, ordered for the lender.
What a property should be worth once renovations are done. The key number in BRRRR.
Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat: add value, refinance to pull cash out, reuse it on the next deal.
Living in a property you own while renting the other rooms or units to cover the mortgage.
vocab.example: Rent 3 rooms at $700 vs $2,300 payment: you pay $200.

vocab.definition: List of every tenant with rent, deposit, lease dates and balance owed.
Money a tenant pays upfront to cover damage or unpaid rent. State law sets limits and return deadlines.
Person or company you pay to handle tenants, rent and repairs. Often 8-10% of rent.
A legal claim on property for a debt, such as a mortgage or unpaid taxes. It must be cleared to sell cleanly.
Legal ownership of a property. A title search checks for liens or ownership problems before you buy.
Fees paid to finish a purchase or refinance: lender, title, appraisal, recording and prepaid items.
What you paid for a property plus certain purchase costs and improvements. Used for depreciation and gains.
Yearly tax deduction for wear on the building, not the land: 27.5 years for rentals. Taxed back partly when you sell.
The IRS form where you report rental income and expenses each year.
Swap one investment property for another and defer the tax on the gain, if strict deadlines are met.
vocab.example: Name new property in 45 days, close within 180.

vocab.definition: A legal entity that can own property and may limit personal liability. Costs fees and can complicate loans.
Lease where the tenant pays rent plus taxes, insurance and maintenance. Common in commercial real estate.
